desc:
A map is an n x n grid of cells with coordinates (x, y), where 0 ≤ x, y < n. The array points lists markers as [x, y] pairs; several markers may lie on the same cell and each one counts.

Each query is [x1, y1, x2, y2] and asks how many markers lie in the rectangle x1 ≤ x ≤ x2, y1 ≤ y ≤ y2 (borders included). Return the answers in query order.

n = 4
points = [[0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 1], [3, 2]]
queries = [[0, 0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 3, 3], [2, 0, 3, 1]]
result = [3, 3, 0]
constraints: 0 ≤ x1 ≤ x2 < n and 0 ≤ y1 ≤ y2 < n
hints: Checking every marker for every query costs O(points * queries) in total. The map is small, so think about the grid itself.
Turn the markers into a grid of counts: cnt[x][y] is the number of markers on that cell. Now each query asks for a rectangle sum over this grid.
Build a 2-D prefix table over cnt and answer every query with the four-term formula in O(1).
editorial: Create an (n + 1) x (n + 1) table P where P[x+1][y+1] starts as the number of markers on cell (x, y). Then convert it into a 2-D prefix table by adding the table above and to the left and subtracting the overlap, so that P[a][b] counts the markers with x < a and y < b.
A query is answered by inclusion-exclusion: P[x2+1][y2+1] - P[x1][y2+1] - P[x2+1][y1] + P[x1][y1]. Multiple markers on one cell are handled naturally because the counts are added, not set.
Time O(n<sup>2</sup> + p + q), space O(n<sup>2</sup>). This trade of memory for speed works because the coordinates are small; with huge coordinates one would sort and compress them first.
